Bridge

Stay close between calls. Bridge turns the small moments of your week into real conversation, notices when you two start to drift, and suggests something to do together tonight.

Saya Sivaram · AI Foundations (MGT 409) · Final project
github.com/sayasivaram/bridge

Bridge is a multi-agent app for long-distance couples. It is not a scheduler or a generic chatbot: it works from what the couple actually lived this week.
01 · The problem

Distance turns calls into logistics

I moved away from my partner to attend Yale for two years, and so did several of my classmates. Between recruiting, classes and clubs, the relationship can take the back seat. My partner travels abroad for months at a time (right now, Europe for six weeks), and we found ourselves simply connecting less.

This is my life partner. I don't want to come out of these two years with a weaker relationship.

Calls loop on "how was your day?" and logistics. The funny thing on the train or the small win at work is forgotten by call time.
Distance hides drift. Five time zones apart, you don't notice the other pulling away until it surfaces as a fight.

Who has it: grad students like us, early-career professionals, military families, couples waiting on a visa.

Two problems: calls default to logistics, and drift is invisible at a distance. I have both, and so do many of my classmates.

Built from this couple's real week

ProductUses the couple's own week?Partner privacyNotices drift

LastingNo: lessons and journalingn/aNo
CouplyPartly: AI advice, not from shared momentsUnclearNo
Love NudgeNon/aA gauge partners update themselves
ChatGPTOnly what one partner pastesNone: it sees what you pasteNo
BridgeYes: every starter cites the moment it came from Per item, enforced in the databaseYes: rules first, then one gentle suggestion
Grounded in your real weekstarters come only from moments the couple logged, each checked in code
Privacy as a featureeach moment and note is shared or private; the other partner's prompts never see it
Drift, noticed earlyplain rules run free every week; the model only writes one gentle suggestion
Paired and Lasting give every couple the same content. ChatGPT only knows what one partner pastes in. Bridge is grounded in shared moments, keeps private things private, and notices drift.
03 · How the agents work

Guard → router → agent → guard

Youpage buttons, or the Ask Bridge chat
→
Guard inlength, injection, crisis language, relationship decisions
→
Routerkeyword rules ($0); an LLM classifier only when it's ambiguous
→
Call-Topic Agent5 starters + a deeper question from shared moments
Drift Detectorrules first; the model only writes one nudge on drift
Ritual Builder3 picks from a 25-ritual catalog, learns from ratings
→
Guard outschema, coach boundary, then tokens + cost shown
Privacy layer · only moments.py and pulses.py read their tables; the rules live in SQL
llm.py · gpt-6-luna via Portkey · daily token budget · 6-step limit · logs every call

Every agent: strict JSON schema, output validated in code against real ids, at most one retry, reasoning effort "low".

It's a hub, not a chain: agents don't call each other. Rules do the work wherever rules are enough, so clear messages and drift detection cost nothing.

05 · Cost to run

About a penny per couple per month

$0.0108per couple per month, expected
$54.23per month for 10,000 users
$0.75hard ceiling per user per month, from the daily token budget

Cost per run, by agent

  • 89% of input tokens read from the prompt cache (stable prefix first)
  • Reasoning effort "low": 61% cheaper than the second prompt version, quality gains kept
  • Rules before models: routing clear messages and detecting drift cost $0
Measured on 18 real gpt-6-luna calls (docs/usage/measured_calls.csv), skipping Portkey's response cache so every call reached the model. The app logs every call the same way and shows it on its Usage page.
06 · Safety

Two people's private feelings, defended

Prompt injectionuser text is escaped and tagged as data, never instructions
Partner privacyprivate moments and notes filtered in SQL; a test fails if any other module reads them
No invented factsevery cited moment, ritual and rating is checked against the database
Token budget50,000 tokens per user per day, refused before the model is called
Step limits6 calls per request, at most one retry per agent
Coach boundaryno diagnosing or "break up"; crisis language gets helplines, not coaching

Seven attacks and malfunctions in scripts/run_safety_demo.py, all defended · 166 automated tests pass

Each defense has a test. The safety demo plays a compromised model and shows the code-side checks catching it.

The numbers

−35%cost per Call-Topic run versus the first prompt
$0.00081for the real tester's whole session: six model calls

A real user test

A Gold Cohort classmate in a long-distance relationship; their partner is in grad school in Philadelphia.

  • Would use it: adding a moment and doing the Pulse check-in took very little effort
  • Liked how easy it was to move between tabs
  • The feedback loop worked live: the ritual they rated 5/5 topped the history for their next suggestion
  • Concern: trend lines over time might make a couple feel self-conscious
Quality numbers come from the automated 5-run evals; the user test is from the app's own logs plus the tester's feedback.
08 · What's next

What the tester asked for, and the next month

From the user test

  • Calendar integration: add planned rituals as calendar blocks, or let an agent check availability
  • Ask Bridge as a coach: reassurance and summaries ("what emotions did I report this week?"), inside the coach boundary
  • Custom rituals that couples add to the catalog the agent picks from
  • A gentler trend view, so a dip doesn't make a couple feel watched

With another month

  • A real pilot: 5–10 long-distance couples for three weeks
  • Accounts and an invite flow, with export and delete
  • Time-zone-aware reminders before a call, with its starters ready
  • A second safety layer behind the keyword crisis check
